items.stem: Which of the following best describes "irredentism"?
options: A claim to territory inhabited by people of the same nationality but ruled by another state, e.g. Argentina’s claim to the Malvinas/Falklands
A cause of war arising from conflicting belief systems, such as communism versus nationalism in the Chinese Civil War
Irregular warfare by small, mobile groups using ambush, sabotage and hit-and-run tactics and relying on popular support, as in Mao’s strategy against the Japanese
The treaties of the Washington Conference (1921–22), including the Five-Power naval treaty and the Nine-Power Treaty guaranteeing China’s integrity, which regulated the Pacific until the 1930s
items.answer: A claim to territory inhabited by people of the same nationality but ruled by another state, e.g. Argentina’s claim to the Malvinas/Falklands
items.markingKey: A. "irredentism" is a claim to territory inhabited by people of the same nationality but ruled by another state, e.g. Argentina’s claim to the Malvinas/Falklands.

items.stem: Briefly explain why ideology was a major cause of the Spanish Civil War.
items.answer: Spain was polarised between the left (socialists, communists, anarchists) supporting land reform, secularism and regional autonomy, and the right (monarchists, the Falange, the Church, army) defending tradition; the Popular Front victory of February 1936 convinced the right that revolution threatened.

(2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the Iran–Iraq War (1980–1988) and explain what it reveals about the interaction of territorial, ideological and political causes.
items.answer: Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980, hoping to exploit the chaos after the 1979 revolution; the war lasted eight years and killed hundreds of thousands. Territory (Shatt al-Arab, Khuzestan), ideology (fear of Khomeini exporting Shi’a revolution to Iraq) and Saddam’s ambition to lead the Arab world combined.

items.stem: Examine the economic and political causes of two 20th-century wars, each chosen from a different region. [15]
items.answer: In both wars economic pressures were real, but political calculations by leaders were decisive.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the Argentine junta invaded the Falklands in 1982.
items.answer: Galtieri’s junta faced economic crisis (inflation above 100 per cent) and growing protest; a popular nationalist cause could rally support, and the junta believed Britain – which had announced the withdrawal of HMS Endurance – would not fight.

items.stem: Briefly explain why political causes of war are often linked to domestic crises.
items.answer: Leaders facing unrest may use war to rally nationalism and divert attention, as with the Argentine junta in 1982 or arguably Saddam after the Iranian Revolution threatened his regime.

items.stem: Distinguish between the causes of a civil war and the causes of an interstate war.
items.answer: Interstate wars arise from disputes between states (territory, security, alliances), while civil wars arise from internal divisions over power, ideology, ethnicity or region, often with foreign involvement.
items.markingKey: Interstate wars arise from disputes between states (territory, security, alliances), while civil wars arise from internal divisions over power, ideology, ethnicity or region, often with foreign involvement. items.stem: With reference to the Falklands/Malvinas War (1982), explain how it illustrates political and territorial causes of war.
items.answer: Argentina occupied the islands on 2 April 1982; Britain sent a task force and recaptured them after 74 days of fighting. Argentina’s long-standing territorial claim was activated by the junta’s domestic crisis, while Thatcher’s government saw the defence of sovereignty as essential.
items.markingKey: Context (Argentina occupied the islands on 2 April 1982; Britain sent a task force and recaptured them after 74 days of fighting.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: "Ideological causes were more important than territorial causes in 20th-century wars." Discuss.
items.answer: Ideology and territory were usually intertwined; their relative importance varies by war and region.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Spanish and Chinese civil wars driven by ideology; Cold War conflicts (Korea, Vietnam); Nazi racial ideology in 1939. Arguments against: Iran–Iraq (Shatt al-Arab), Falklands, Chaco War over territory; territory often the issue even in ideological wars (Korea’s division); leaders’ use of ideology to justify territorial aims. items.stem: Define the term "limited war".
items.answer: A war in which the aims, geographical area or weapons used are deliberately restricted, such as the Korean War or the Falklands War

items.stem: "Guerrilla warfare cannot win wars on its own." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It often wins when combined with political mobilisation and later conventional operations, as in China (1945–49) and Vietnam (Dien Bien Phu, 1954).
items.markingKey: It often wins when combined with political mobilisation and later conventional operations, as in China (1945–49) and Vietnam (Dien Bien Phu, 1954). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why guerrilla warfare relies on popular support.
items.answer: Guerrillas need civilians for food, shelter, recruits and intelligence; as Mao put it, the guerrilla must move among the people as a fish swims in the sea.

items.stem: Explain why the Treaty of Versailles is often described as a weak foundation for peace.
items.answer: It was harsh enough to cause lasting German resentment but not harsh enough to permanently weaken Germany; it was not enforced consistently; and the USA did not ratify it.

items.stem: Explain why historians disagree about when the Second World War began.
items.answer: A Eurocentric view dates it from 1 September 1939; others argue for 1937 (full Sino-Japanese War) or even 1931 (Manchuria), and some see 1941 as the point when separate regional wars became a global war.

items.answer: The Locarno Treaties

items.stem: Briefly explain why the invasion of Poland led to a general European war when earlier German expansion had not.
items.answer: Britain and France had guaranteed Poland after Prague; appeasement was discredited; the Nazi–Soviet Pact removed any hope of a deal; and Hitler did not believe the Western powers would fight.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Polish crisis over Danzig (1939) and explain what it reveals about short-term causes of the Second World War in Europe.
items.answer: Hitler demanded the return of the Free City of Danzig and an extraterritorial road across the Polish Corridor; Poland, backed by Britain, refused. The dispute provided the immediate issue for war, but Hitler had already decided to destroy Poland (Case White).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the view that war was caused by structural factors and the intentionalist view of the outbreak of war.
items.answer: Intentionalists blame Hitler’s ideology and plans; structural explanations stress Versailles, the Depression, the failure of the League and the international system that allowed aggression.

items.stem: "Most 20th-century wars had a single main cause." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Most wars were multi-causal: for example, the Iran–Iraq War combined territorial disputes, ideological fears of Khomeini’s revolution, ethnic and religious divisions and personal ambition.

items.stem: Explain why the Korean War is considered a limited war.
items.answer: Both sides restricted their aims and means: the USA did not use nuclear weapons or bomb Chinese bases in Manchuria, the USSR did not openly commit troops, and the war ended with a return to roughly the pre-war border.

items.stem: "The Second World War began simultaneously in Asia and Europe in 1939." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The war in Asia had been underway since 1937; the two wars merged into one global conflict in December 1941 after Pearl Harbor and Germany’s declaration of war on the USA.
items.markingKey: The war in Asia had been underway since 1937; the two wars merged into one global conflict in December 1941 after Pearl Harbor and Germany’s declaration of war on the USA. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the Polish crisis over Danzig (1939) as an example, explain short-term causes of the Second World War in Europe.
items.answer: Hitler demanded the return of the Free City of Danzig and an extraterritorial road across the Polish Corridor; Poland, backed by Britain, refused. The dispute provided the immediate issue for war, but Hitler had already decided to destroy Poland (Case White).

items.stem: Briefly describe the Algerian War of Independence (1954–1962) and explain what it reveals about guerrilla war and decolonisation.
items.answer: The FLN waged a guerrilla and urban terror campaign against French rule; France used counter-insurgency tactics including torture; Algeria gained independence in 1962. The FLN could not defeat the French army militarily, but its guerrilla campaign made French rule politically unsustainable.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that guerrilla warfare was the most effective strategy for weaker forces in 20th-century wars? [15]
items.answer: Guerrilla warfare was effective when tied to political mobilisation and outside support, but rarely decisive alone.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "economic cause"?
options: A cause of war arising from competition for resources, markets or economic survival, such as oil in the Gulf War of 1991
A war in which states mobilise their entire economies, populations and resources, and civilians become targets, as in the Second World War
Irregular warfare by small, mobile groups using ambush, sabotage and hit-and-run tactics and relying on popular support, as in Mao’s strategy against the Japanese
A cause of war arising from disputes over land, borders or strategic territory, such as the Shatt al-Arab waterway in the Iran–Iraq War
items.answer: A cause of war arising from competition for resources, markets or economic survival, such as oil in the Gulf War of 1991
items.markingKey: A. "economic cause" is a cause of war arising from competition for resources, markets or economic survival, such as oil in the Gulf War of 1991.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the intentionalist view of the outbreak of war and the view that war was caused by structural factors.
items.answer: Intentionalists blame Hitler’s ideology and plans; structural explanations stress Versailles, the Depression, the failure of the League and the international system that allowed aggression.

items.answer: Most wars were multi-causal: for example, the Iran–Iraq War combined territorial disputes, ideological fears of Khomeini’s revolution, ethnic and religious divisions and personal ambition.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that ideological causes were more important than territorial causes in 20th-century wars.
items.answer: Ideology and territory were usually intertwined; their relative importance varies by war and region.
